title: Solitaire
blurb: Klondike, draw one or three
why: The card game that came with Windows 3.0 in 1990.

title: Solitaire
blurb: Klondike, draw one or three
why: The card game that came with Windows 3.0 in 1990.

title: FreeCell
blurb: The numbered deals, every one winnable but one
why: Microsoft numbered its deals, and only one of the first 32,000 cannot be won.

title: Spider
blurb: Two decks, runs of one suit, clear all eight
why: Two decks and one goal: build eight runs from king down to ace.

title: Hearts
blurb: You against three, dodge the queen
why: A trick-taking game where the aim is to take as few points as you can.

title: Pyramid
blurb: Pairs that make 13
why: Take pairs that add to 13 from a pyramid of 28 cards.

title: Golf
blurb: One higher or lower, no wrap
why: Clear seven columns of five cards before the stock runs out.

title: TriPeaks
blurb: Three peaks, wrap round, keep the streak
why: Clear three peaks of cards, and every card in a row keeps the streak alive.

title: Spades
blurb: Partners, bids, Nil and bags
why: A partnership trick-taking game from 1930s America where spades are always trump.

title: Euchre
blurb: Bowers, trump and going alone, to 10
why: A trick-taking game of the American Midwest, played with just 24 cards.

title: Gin Rummy
blurb: Knock, go gin or catch them with an undercut
why: A two-player rummy game from the early 1900s.

title: Cribbage
blurb: Peg to 121 on a board drawn here
why: Said to have been invented by the poet Sir John Suckling in the 1600s, and scored on a peg board.

title: Crazy Eights
blurb: Match suit or rank, eights are wild
why: The shedding game behind Uno: every eight is wild.

title: Durak
blurb: The Russian game: beat it, throw in, never be the fool
why: Russia's best-loved card game: whoever is left holding cards is the durak, the fool.

title: Scopa
blurb: The Italian fishing game, with an Italian deck
why: Italy's national card game, played with a 40-card Italian deck.

title: Reversi
blurb: Flip the board, against the computer or a friend
why: Invented in England in 1883; Othello is its modern cousin.

title: Checkers
blurb: English draughts, captures are compulsory
why: English draughts was proved in 2007 to be a draw with perfect play.

title: Chess
blurb: Our own engine, four levels, no download
why: Its modern rules took shape in Europe around 1500.

title: Go
blurb: 9x9 and 13x13, territory scoring, komi 6.5
why: Over 2,500 years old, and one of the oldest board games still played.

title: Xiangqi
blurb: Chinese chess, with the river and the flying general
why: China's chess, with a river across the middle of the board.

title: Shogi
blurb: Japanese chess with drops, and a small 5x5 board
why: Japan's chess, where captured pieces change sides and can be dropped back in.

title: Hex
blurb: Link your two sides, no draws, swap rule optional
why: Invented separately by Piet Hein in 1942 and John Nash in 1948.

title: Gomoku
blurb: Five in a row on a 15x15 board
why: Played with Go stones: the first to make five in a row wins.

title: Nine Men's Morris
blurb: Make mills, fly when you are down to three
why: An ancient game, with boards scratched into stone since Roman times.

title: Four in a Row
blurb: Drop discs, line up four
why: Sold as Connect Four since 1974, and a win for whoever moves first with perfect play.

title: Dots and Boxes
blurb: Close boxes, move again, 4 to 7 dots
why: A pencil-and-paper game that the mathematician Edouard Lucas described in 1889.

title: Backgammon
blurb: Race home, hit blots, optional doubling cube
why: Its ancestors go back about 5,000 years.

title: Mancala
blurb: Oware and Kalah, sow and capture
why: One of the oldest games still played, with sowing boards found across Africa and Asia.

title: Ludo
blurb: Roll a six, race round the cross, send rivals home
why: Descended from India's Pachisi and patented in England in 1896.

title: Chinese Checkers
blurb: Hop marbles across the star, two to six players
why: Not Chinese: it came from Germany in 1892 as Sternhalma.

title: Dominoes
blurb: Draw and Block, against one to three computers
why: Tiles with pips, played across Europe since the 1700s.

title: Mahjong
blurb: Three layouts, every deal can be cleared
why: The solitaire version matches tiles from a pile; the four-player game is a different one.

title: Minesweeper
blurb: Beginner to Expert, first click always safe
why: A Windows staple since the early 1990s.

title: Sudoku
blurb: Four levels, every puzzle has one solution
why: Named in Japan in 1984, and every puzzle here has exactly one solution.

blurb: Slide and merge tiles, one undo
why: Written in a weekend in 2014 by Gabriele Cirulli.

title: Five Letters
blurb: Guess the word in six tries, daily or practice
why: Find the five-letter word in six tries.

title: Wiki Race
blurb: Get from one article to another by links alone, in your own Wikipedia
why: Players race between Wikipedia articles using only links; here it runs on your own library.

title: Letter by Letter
blurb: Guess the word, keep the balloon up; words from your Wiktionary
why: Guess the word a letter at a time, with words and meanings from your Wiktionary.

title: Quizzical
blurb: Questions made from the articles and words in your library
why: Questions made from the articles in your own library.

title: Jigsaw
blurb: A picture from your Wikipedia, 12 to 100 pieces
why: Jigsaw puzzles began as maps cut into pieces to teach geography, in the 1760s.

title: Snake
blurb: Eat, grow, speed up; walls or wrap-around
why: Descended from the 1976 arcade game Blockade, and on Nokia phones from 1997.

title: Bricks
blurb: Paddle and ball, eight levels, angle by where it lands
why: Descended from Atari's Breakout of 1976.

title: Fifteen
blurb: Slide the tiles back into order
why: The 15 puzzle craze swept America and Europe in 1880.

title: Same Game
blurb: Clear blocks of matching colour
why: Invented in 1985 by Kuniaki Moribe as Chain Shot!

title: Pegs
blurb: Jump pegs over pegs until one is left
why: Peg solitaire, a game for one that dates back to at least 17th-century France.

title: Pattern
blurb: Use the row and column clues to reveal a picture
why: Nonograms, a picture puzzle that took off in Japan in the late 1980s.

title: Slant
blurb: Fill with diagonals so numbers touch that many
why: Known in Japan as Gokigen Naname.

title: Light Up
blurb: Place lamps to light the room, none lighting another
why: Known in Japan as Akari.

title: Loopy
blurb: Draw one loop; numbers count each cell's sides
why: Known in Japan as Slitherlink.

title: Bridges
blurb: Join the islands with bridges to match their numbers
why: Known in Japan as Hashiwokakero.

title: Galaxies
blurb: Split into regions that look the same turned half way
why: Known in Japan as Tentaisho, the heavenly bodies game.

title: Rectangles
blurb: One rectangle per number, with a matching area
why: Known in Japan as Shikaku, the game of squares.

title: Keen
blurb: Fill the grid; each cage must make its number
why: In the family of KenKen, invented in 2004 by Tetsuya Miyamoto.

title: Unequal
blurb: Fill the grid, obeying the greater-than signs
why: Known as Futoshiki, which is Japanese for inequality.

title: Pearl
blurb: Draw a loop through the pearls as marked
why: Known in Japan as Masyu.

title: Range
blurb: Shade squares so each number sees that many
why: Known in Japan as Kuromasu.

title: Singles
blurb: Shade repeats; shaded squares never touch
why: Known in Japan as Hitori, which means alone.

title: Filling
blurb: Every region holds a number equal to its size
why: Known in Japan as Fillomino.

title: Black Box
blurb: Find the hidden balls by firing beams in
why: Devised by Eric Solomon in 1977.

title: Guess
blurb: Crack the hidden colour code
why: The code-breaking game sold as Mastermind since 1972.

title: Flip
blurb: Light every square by flipping groups of them
why: A cousin of Lights Out.

title: Unruly
blurb: Two colours, no three in a row, balanced lines
why: Also called Binairo or Takuzu.

title: Yacht
blurb: Thirteen rows, five dice, solo or against computers
why: The public-domain dice game that later became Yahtzee.

title: Liar's Dice
blurb: Bid, bluff and call the lie, two to six players
why: Bluffing with dice under cups, played across South America as Perudo.

title: Fleet
blurb: Hide your ships, hunt the computer's
why: Hunting hidden ships on a grid began as a pencil-and-paper game before the First World War.

title: Code Breaker
blurb: Crack the four-peg code, with shapes as well as colours
why: Guessing a hidden code from clues goes back to the paper game Bulls and Cows.

title: Pinball
blurb: Flippers, bumpers, lanes and multiball on one table
why: Flippers arrived in 1947; before that, pinball was mostly luck.

title: Rocks
blurb: Drift, turn and shoot; rocks split, a saucer shoots back
why: Drift, turn and fire as every rock you hit splits into smaller ones.

title: Last Line
blurb: Drone rows descend, shields wear away, hold the line
why: Rows of invaders marching down the screen made the shooter a genre in 1978.

title: Lander
blurb: Thrust and rotate down onto a pad before the fuel is gone
why: Land softly with the fuel you have, as Apollo crews did on the Moon.

title: Paddles
blurb: Two-paddle tennis, against the computer or a friend
why: Two paddles and a ball: the game that started the video game industry in 1972.

title: Memory
blurb: Match the pairs; animals and shapes
why: Concentration, the card game of turning over pairs, is played by children everywhere.

title: Echo
blurb: Repeat the growing sequence of pads
why: Repeat the growing sequence of colours and tones.

title: Noughts and Crosses
blurb: Three in a row, against an easy or a perfect computer
why: Played perfectly, noughts and crosses is always a draw.

title: Koi-Koi
blurb: Hanafuda flower cards, make yaku, call koi-koi
why: Hanafuda, Japan's flower cards, came about when Western playing cards were banned in the 1600s.

title: Truco
blurb: Argentine bluffing game with envido, to 15 or 30
why: The bluffing card game of Argentina and Uruguay, played with a Spanish deck.

title: Belote
blurb: Partners, trump, belote and rebelote
why: France's most played card game, partners bidding for trump.

title: Skat
blurb: Three players: bid, take the skat, suit, grand or null
why: Germany's national card game, invented in Altenburg around 1810.

title: Teen Patti
blurb: Blind or seen, side show and show, with chips
why: India's three-card game, a close cousin of three-card brag.

title: Bridge
blurb: Bid, play and defend with a computer partner
why: Contract bridge, settled in its modern form by Harold Vanderbilt in 1925.

title: Texas Hold’em
blurb: Chips, blinds, all in and side pots
why: Texas Hold'em, played here for chips only.

title: Blackjack
blurb: Beat the dealer to 21, split and double
why: Twenty-one against the dealer, with a basic-strategy hint if you want one.

title: Canasta
blurb: Meld, freeze the pile, go out to 5000
why: Canasta came from Uruguay in the 1940s and swept the world within a decade.

title: Big Two
blurb: Climb with pairs and fives, twos are high
why: Big Two, the climbing game played across southern China and Taiwan.

title: Tien Len
blurb: Runs, pairs in a row and chops
why: Tien Len, Vietnam's national card game, where the two is the highest card.

title: Janggi
blurb: Korean chess: palaces, cannons that need a screen, bikjang
why: Korean chess, where the generals stay in their palaces and cannons need a screen to jump.

title: Makruk
blurb: Thai chess: Khon, Met and Bia, a move-limit count
why: Thai chess, close to the Indian game that chess grew from.

title: International Draughts
blurb: Flying kings, take the most pieces, men capture backwards
why: International draughts on 10 by 10, the version played across Europe and Africa.

title: Hnefatafl
blurb: Copenhagen rules: the king runs for a corner
why: The Viking board game: the king escapes to a corner or is captured.

title: Hnefatafl
blurb: Copenhagen rules: the king runs for a corner
why: The Viking board game: the king escapes to a corner or is captured.

title: Royal Game of Ur
blurb: Four dice, rosettes, a race 4,500 years old
why: Played in Mesopotamia 4,500 years ago; its rules survive on a clay tablet.

title: Snakes and Ladders
blurb: Two to four players, our own drawn board
why: Snakes and Ladders began in India as Moksha Patam, a game about virtue and vice.

title: Carrom
blurb: Flick the striker, pocket your coins, cover the queen
why: Flick and pocket on a wooden board, played in homes across South Asia.

title: Mahjong for Four
blurb: Hong Kong old style against three computers
why: Mahjong for four, the tile game played at tables across China and beyond.

title: Circuit
blurb: Four tracks, rival cars and a ghost of your best lap
why: Atari's Gran Trak 10, in 1974, put a wheel and pedals on an arcade cabinet.

title: Road Rush
blurb: Hills, curves and traffic against the clock
why: Arcade racers of the 1980s faked a 3D road by scaling flat strips of it.

title: Hopper
blurb: Run, jump and stomp through six short levels
why: Platformers took a screen full of ledges and made jumping the whole game.

title: Muncher
blurb: Eat every dot while four chasers hunt you
why: Maze chases were an arcade staple by 1980, each chaser with its own way of hunting you.

title: Crossing
blurb: Hop a critter over roads and rivers
why: A 1981 arcade game about nothing more than getting across the road.

title: Blast
blurb: Grid bombers, blocks and chain reactions, up to two on one keyboard
why: Bombs that blast in four directions and set each other off made a whole genre of grid fights.

title: Quest
blurb: A tiny top-down adventure: sword, keys, a door and a boss
why: Sword, key, locked door: the shape of top-down adventures since the early 1980s.

title: Zimi Pet
blurb: Hatch an egg and raise a small creature over real days
why: Pocket pets from the late 1990s asked only that you come back and feed them.

title: ZimiKart
blurb: Eight critters, six tracks, drift for a boost
why: Kart racers fake a 3D road by tilting one flat picture of the track, a trick the 1990s consoles did in hardware.

title: Chess Puzzles
blurb: 15,000 rated puzzles from Lichess, with your own rating
why: Lichess gives each puzzle a rating from how many players solved it, and publishes them all as open data.

title: Opening Trainer
blurb: 3,800 named openings: play your side of the line
why: Opening names and their ECO codes, A00 to E99, are how chess players have filed the first moves for generations.

title: Go Problems
blurb: Life and death: make a group live, or kill it
why: Tsumego are Go's life-and-death problems, the classic way to learn to read ahead.

title: Sokoban
blurb: Push the crates onto the rings: 300 graded levels
why: Sokoban is Japanese for warehouse keeper, and Thinking Rabbit published the game in 1982.
